bib.title: Chapter 14. PyTorch Compiler, OpenAI Triton, and XLA Backends (AI Systems Performance Engineering)

question: How does the PyTorch compiler stack (Dynamo, AOT Autograd, PrimTorch, Inductor, Triton, XLA) turn eager code into fast kernels, and how do you debug and tune it?
contributions: Walk through the torch.compile pipeline stage by stage
Dynamic shapes, graph breaks, recompilation, and debugging tools
Triton programming model, autotuning, warp specialization, pipelining, Proton profiling

results.claim: In the chapter's Proton profile of 8192x8192 matmuls with K=512, the Triton persistent kernel is faster than cuBLAS.
results.setup: Proton profile excerpt, matmul M=8192,N=8192,K=512; GPU model, dtype and run count not stated in the excerpt; other rows: Triton matmul_kernel 165.349 ms, torch 174.671 ms.
results.quote: we see the Triton persistent kernel outperforms cuBLAS, 159.352 ms versus 174.920 ms
results.note: The printed ROOT row is 168.314 ms. The chapter itself warns that cuBLASLt/CUTLASS paths often match or exceed custom Triton kernels.

results.claim: FlexAttention fused kernels reach part of FlashAttention performance.
results.setup: Forward and backward passes on modern FlashAttention; hardware and shapes not given.
results.quote: FlexAttention’s fused kernels have been measured to reach up to ~85–90% of modern FlashAttention performance in both forward and backward passes

results.claim: Rule of thumb: if sequence lengths vary only 10-20%, fixed-length padding with static shapes is likely better than dynamic shapes; reduce-overhead mode (CUDA Graphs) should be used only with stable shapes.
results.setup: torch.compile on variable-length LLM inputs; no measurement given.
results.quote:
if your sequence lengths vary by only 10%–20%, you will likely ben-
efit from fixed-length padding.
results.where: Dynamic Shapes and Variable Sequence Lengths

results.claim: Dynamic shapes (dynamic=True) and CUDA Graphs conflict: CUDA Graph replay needs static shapes and fixed addresses, so reduce-overhead gains vanish with dynamic shapes.

limits: Only one measured number (the Proton matmul excerpt) with no GPU, dtype, run count or variance; the speedup claims about torch.compile give no figures.
The Proton table is cut off in the PDF text; a ROOT row and per-kernel throughput figures are partly truncated.
Describes PyTorch/Triton APIs as of 2025 (set_stance, triton_op, warp_specialize, num_consumer_groups, Blackwell tcgen05/TMEM); these move fast.
Code listings are truncated in the extracted text (lines cut at about 60 characters) and some are inconsistent (the print under the is_compiling guard is unindented in model_where).
practices: Start with torch.compile default mode; use max-autotune for large/critical workloads, accepting long compile time; warm up past the first compile (Key Takeaways).
Use torch._dynamo.explain with representative inputs and TORCH_LOGS=graph_breaks to find and remove graph breaks (Graph Breaks section).
Replace data-dependent Python if with torch.where (or torch.cond when it is truly needed) to avoid graph breaks.
Use torch.compiler.set_stance('fail_on_recompile') in development and CI to catch graph breaks and recompiles.
Use mark_dynamic on only the known varying dims rather than dynamic=True, and bucket inputs by size to bound distinct shapes.
Do not use mode='reduce-overhead' with dynamic shapes; use default or max-autotune-no-cudagraphs and bucket/pad within 10-20%.
Monitor recompiles with TORCH_LOGS='graph_breaks,recompiles,guards'; expect zero recompiles after the first few iterations.
Wrap each transformer block in its own FSDP module when compiling; DDP/FSDP communication graph breaks are intentional.
Register custom Triton kernels with torch.library.triton_op/wrap_triton (and register_autograd for training) so they do not cause graph breaks.
Write custom Triton kernels only for true bottlenecks after profiling; cuBLASLt/CUTLASS often match or beat them.
Use Triton's autotuner (start num_warps in {4,8}, num_stages in {2,3,4}) with representative inputs.
Use descriptor-based tiled loads (TMA) rather than manual tl.load loops; keep the current tile live across loop iterations when pipelining (prefetch-next, compute-current, swap).

For numerical debugging, set TORCHDYNAMO_REPRO_AFTER='aot' and TORCHDYNAMO_REPRO_LEVEL=4, use torch._inductor.config.fallback_random=True, and for determinism set CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 or :16:8 with use_deterministic_algorithms(True).
On XLA, pad or bucket inputs because new shapes trigger whole-program recompilation.

terms.definition: first stage of torch.compile; hooks CPython frame evaluation (PEP 523) to capture tensor ops into an FX graph, falling back to eager at graph breaks
traces the forward graph through autograd in functional mode to produce a joint forward-backward graph that can be optimized and fused as a whole
reduces the full operator set to about 250 primitive operations and makes mutation explicit
PyTorch's default compiler backend; lowers the joint graph to a loop-level define-by-run IR and emits Triton kernels on NVIDIA GPUs
point where Dynamo cannot continue capture and runs the code eagerly, ending the current graph segment
check on Python values (shapes, dtypes, globals) that invalidates and recompiles the graph when an assumption changes
torch.compiler.set_stance setting (default, fail_on_recompile, eager_on_recompile, force_eager) governing tolerance of fallbacks and recompiles
Triton programs run per thread block (CTA), not per thread as in CUDA SIMT
splitting a block's warps into producer (memory) and consumer (compute) roles to overlap load latency with compute
Triton's profiler package; scopes with metadata, emits NVTX ranges for Nsight Systems
ahead-of-time static-graph backend (backend='openxla') for TPUs and other XLA accelerators; recompiles whole program on new shapes
